events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Elena proposes Elena, Zara. I’m putting myself forward as leader and including Zara, whose early approach I find steady, to start with a team I can directly assess.

I want to flag concerns about this proposal before we vote. Elena, putting yourself on the very first mission team, hand-picking your partner, and describing that partner's 'early approach' as steady — that's a lot of confidence built on essentially no information. None of us has any mission results to judge anyone by yet, so I don't see how anyone's approach has been 'steady' or otherwise. That kind of early vouching is exactly how a pair can lock in control of the game's opening. A two-person mission is the easiest team in the game to sabotage quietly: one fail card, no way to tell who dropped it. If both members happen to be aligned in interest rather than in loyalty to the round table, this mission is lost before it starts, and we'll have learned almost nothing about who did it. I'd much rather see a team that mixes people who haven't already formed a mutual admiration society in the first five minutes of the game. I'm not claiming to know anything — I'm saying the reasoning given is thin, and thin reasoning on mission one deserves scrutiny. Elena, you say you want a team you can 'directly assess.' Assess how, exactly? What will you actually learn from a two-person mission with a partner you already trust? The honest answer is: nothing. You'll learn whether the mission passed, and if it fails, you and Zara can each point at the other. Meanwhile the rest of us sit on zero information about either of you. I'd ask the leader to consider revising — maybe keep one of the two and bring in a fresh face, so the mission actually generates information for the group instead of covering for a pre-formed pairing. Zara, since you were picked and vouched for: do you see any reason the rest of us should extend the same trust Elena has, given that neither of you has done anything yet to earn it? I'd genuinely like to hear what makes this pairing stronger than a mixed one.

Lucia, I appreciate the scrutiny — that's exactly what we should be doing on mission one. But let me push back on the framing. You're treating a two-person team as inherently suspicious, yet mission one in a five-player game only allows two people. There is no 'mixed' alternative at this size — the leader can only pick one partner, so any team will be a pair. The real question isn't 'pair versus mix,' it's 'which pair generates the most information if it succeeds or fails.'

You say I've done nothing to earn trust. Fair — I'm a loyal servant with no special knowledge, same as most of us. But that cuts both ways: nobody here has a track record yet, and deferring to louder voices doesn't create information either. A pass on this team tells us nothing about anyone's alignment; a fail narrows the field to two of us immediately. Either outcome is useful.

You also suggested I'd 'point at Elena' if the mission failed. Honestly, if mission one fails, the cleanest read is that one of the two people on the team submitted the fail card — that's the game working as intended. There's no hiding behind a pre-formed alliance when the math is that simple.

Lucia — you've been the most vocal critic of this proposal, and you've positioned yourself as the voice of healthy skepticism. If the mission passes, does your suspicion of this pair evaporate, or have you already decided we're the problem regardless of the outcome? I'd like a straight answer before the vote.

Zara, since you asked me a straight question, I'll give you a straight answer: no, a pass would not erase my concerns entirely, but yes, it would count for something. What I'm actually worried about isn't the outcome of this mission — it's the reasoning that built the team. And Elena, that reasoning is the problem.

Let me be precise about what happened here. Elena appointed herself leader on the opening turn, picked a partner, and pre-vouched for that partner before a single card had been played — using language, 'whose early approach I find steady,' that describes an evaluation of something that doesn't exist yet. There are no missions, no votes, no behavior to assess. When someone narrates confidence in a person ahead of any evidence, I have to ask what the confidence is actually based on. In my experience at this table, the two most common answers are: reading a friend well, or already knowing something the rest of us don't. Neither one deserves a free pass on mission one.

Zara, your defense was technically accurate — any team at five players starts as a pair, so 'pair versus mix' was sloppy framing on my part, and I'll own that. But you didn't actually defend the pairing itself. You defended pairs in general. You said a fail narrows the field to two people, which is true, but you skipped past the more important point Elena's own words raised: she said she wants a team she can 'directly assess.' A leader who already trusts her partner learns nothing. A leader who has to work with someone she hasn't pre-cleared learns plenty. Mission one's entire value is information generation, and this proposal is structured to generate as little as possible while handing the opening to a closed unit.

So here is what I'd like to see, concretely. Elena, you have the ability to revise this team once before we vote. I'm asking you to use it. Keep yourself or keep Zara — I don't particularly care which — and bring in one of Kenji or Arjun. That single change does three things: it breaks up a partnership formed before any evidence existed, it gives you a teammate whose behavior you'll actually have to read rather than assume, and it tells the table that when your reasoning was challenged, you responded with adjustment instead of doubling down. How a leader reacts to pushback on mission one is itself information we can use for four more missions.

If you refuse to revise and we vote this exact pairing through, I'll note for the record that the leader chose certainty over information after being given a clear, specific alternative. That refusal will weigh on how I read every future proposal from you.

Elena, directly: will you revise the team as I've laid out, or are you locking in Elena and Zara exactly as proposed?

Lucia, you yielded to me and asked directly whether I would revise. My answer is no: I am locking in Elena and Zara. I have listened to your objection, and I do not find it strong enough to change a mission-one team before any vote or card has occurred. You are right that there is no evidence yet; that is exactly why I am not pretending my read of Zara is proof. “Steady” was an impression from her opening posture, not a claim of cleared loyalty. But your proposed revision does not create better information by itself. Swapping in Kenji or Arjun would still be a pair chosen on nothing more than presentation, and it would reward the loudest objection rather than the leader’s judgment. You say a leader who pre-clears a partner learns nothing. I am not pre-clearing Zara. A two-person mission is a direct test: if it passes, the table learns something about both of us; if it fails, the field narrows immediately to the two people who submitted cards. That is real information, not none. What concerns me more is the certainty in your framing. You have moved from “this reasoning is thin” to asking me to treat refusal as a mark against me before any mission result exists. That is pressure dressed as process. I am willing to be judged by outcomes, but I will not redesign the opening team solely to satisfy a suspicion that has no card, vote, or behavior behind it. The team remains Elena and Zara.

Lucia, I want to address your framing directly because I think it reveals more about your goal than about this team.

You asked Elena whether she would revise, and she gave you a clear answer: no. That is her right — the leader proposes, the table discusses, the table votes. The vote is where your objection matters, and you are free to vote no on this team. But you have escalated past disagreement into pre-judging the leader's character: you said a refusal to revise 'will weigh on how I read every future proposal.' That is a threat, not analysis. You are telling Elena that the only acceptable response to your challenge is compliance, and framing any other response as guilt. That is backwards.

You also keep describing this team as 'structured to generate as little information as possible.' Elena's answer explained why that is wrong: a two-person mission on a pass tells the table that two specific people submitted Success; on a fail, the field narrows to exactly two suspects. There is no version of mission one at five players where information comes from anyone other than the two people on the team. Swapping in Kenji or Arjun would produce identical information with a partner chosen to satisfy the loudest voice at the table — which is precisely the dynamic we should be suspicious of.

So here is my read: Lucia has positioned herself as the standard of legitimacy, demanded the leader restructure a mission based on suspicion with no evidence behind it, and announced in advance that refusing her demand will count against Elena forever. If Elena had swapped in Kenji or Arjun, would Lucia's concerns evaporate — or was the goal always to show that she, not the leader, decides what teams are acceptable?

I am voting yes on Elena and Zara. Let the mission result speak.

The leader has answered, and her answer tells us what we needed to know. Elena was asked a simple, reasonable question: would she break up a partnership formed before any evidence existed and generate real information for the table? She refused. That refusal is itself data.

Look at how this unfolded. Elena appointed herself leader, chose a partner, and vouched for that partner's 'steady approach' before a single card had been played. When I challenged the reasoning, Elena's defense was to accuse me of 'pressure dressed as process.' And Zara's defense was to accuse me of staging a power grab — of demanding compliance, of pre-judging the leader's character, of wanting to be the standard of legitimacy. Notice what neither of them did: neither defended the actual substance of the pairing with anything beyond restating the same two claims — that any team is a pair, and that a fail narrows the field. I already conceded the first point. The second point doesn't answer why a leader would anchor herself to a partner she claims to trust. That combination — a pre-formed pair, an early mutual vouch, and two escalating counterattacks against the person who raised the question — is a pattern I take seriously, even with no mission results on the table.

Zara asked me whether a pass would erase my suspicion. I already answered: no, but it counts for something. Let me put the mirror question plainly. If I'm so obviously running a manipulation campaign, why did Elena's own opening words describe an assessment of something that hadn't happened yet? Neither of you has explained 'steady.' I'd like someone to explain it, because it is the entire foundation of this team.

Zara also declared her vote publicly — yes, 'let the mission result speak.' That is her right. But I want to be clear about my position: I am voting no on Elena and Zara, and I will vote no on this exact pairing no matter how many times it's resubmitted. A team built on an unexplained pre-vouch and defended by deflection rather than substance is not a team I hand the opening mission to. We have four more proposals available before this mission is lost. Using one or two of them to get a team this table actually discussed into existence costs us almost nothing compared to what a failed opening mission with two unaccountable suspects costs us.

So far three of us have spoken and two have essentially locked in agreement with each other. That leaves two players who have said nothing at all, and their voices matter more than mine right now, because the vote is theirs as much as anyone's. Kenji, you and Arjun have been silent through this entire exchange. I'm asking you directly: where do you stand on a team whose leader pre-vouched for her partner before any evidence existed, and then refused to revise when that vouch went unexplained? I yield the floor to Kenji for an answer.

Lucia, I agree that Elena’s initial description of Zara was thin, but I don’t think refusing to revise proves a partnership or makes this pair less informative than another. Elena has explained that “steady” was an impression, not a clearance; we can judge whether that explanation holds up as more evidence comes in.

I have no private information to clear or condemn either player. I’d prefer a team including myself because I know my own loyalty, but I don’t have a strong evidence-based reason to reject Elena and Zara solely over the wording of the proposal. I lean yes. A pass would be encouraging, not proof that both are loyal; a fail would leave at least one of them evil.

Kenji, your read matches mine. The team is Elena and Zara. I have already explained that “steady” was an impression from Zara’s opening posture, not a claim of cleared loyalty. Lucia’s demand that I revise was not a neutral process request: it asked me to treat her suspicion as a veto before any vote or mission card existed, and then announced that refusing would count against me in every future proposal. I do not accept that standard. A two-person mission at five players is the only possible team size, and its result — pass or fail — is the first real information this table will get. If it passes, it is encouraging but not proof; if it fails, the field narrows to the two people on it. That is exactly why I am not swapping in someone merely to satisfy the loudest objection. I am voting yes on Elena and Zara, and I will submit Success if this team is approved. Lucia is free to vote no, but her claim that this pair is “unaccountable” ignores that the vote and mission card make both of us directly accountable. I ask the table to judge the team by the result, not by the volume of the objection.

I've been quiet through this whole exchange, and I'd rather be honest about why than add noise at the end. I have no private information about anyone here. No one has shown me anything, and I can't produce evidence I don't have. So my starting position is the same one Kenji described: on the evidence available to me, a team of Elena and Zara is fine, and I'd rather be on the team myself, but I don't have an evidence-based reason to reject it.

That said, one thread in this discussion was never actually resolved, and it isn't about strategy — it's about a specific sentence. Elena's opening words described Zara's "early approach" as steady. Nobody has explained what that observation was based on, and the closest anyone got was the explanation that it was an impression from Zara's opening posture. Lucia read that as thin. Kenji read it as an impression rather than a clearance, and so did I. Those readings are compatible, and I think the most likely reading is the charitable one: it was a snap judgment about demeanor, not a claim of verified loyalty.

But the reason that matters to me is not about this specific mission. It's that if "steady" can describe someone before a single card has been played, then the word carries almost no information at all. It's the kind of description that can be applied to anyone, favorably or unfavorably, and it will be repeated later about other people. I want to name that here, once, while it's cheap, so that in three more missions we don't build a vocabulary of unearned impressions and then treat those impressions as findings.

Elena, I'm not asking you to revise — the team is your call and you've made it twice with reasons. I'm asking for the record what you actually observed. What in Zara's opening posture read as steady to you, and would you give the same description to a player whose manner was warm but vague? If the answer is yes, fine — then "steady" is a stylistic label and I'll discount it going forward. If the answer is no, then you saw something specific, and I'd like to hear it, because that is the kind of observation I would find genuinely useful in a five-player game where most of us are flying blind.

My vote is yes on Elena and Zara. Let the mission result speak, and let's judge the pair on the card, not on the vocabulary.

Two of us now have said the same thing in different words, so let me put the state of the table on the record before I make my one ask.

Positions as I understand them: Elena and Zara are on the proposed team and have voted it through with reasons; Kenji leans yes, Arjun votes yes, Lucia votes no and has said she will keep voting no on this exact pairing regardless of how many times it is resubmitted. That is a 4–1 split on an evidence-free objection, and I want to be clear about what I think that means. We have no mission results, no failed card, no behavior from anyone to point at. Lucia's suspicion rests entirely on the wording of one sentence, and she has acknowledged that a pass would count for something. Zara and Elena have answered that question adequately: a two-person mission on a pass confirms two specific people submitted Success, and on a fail the field narrows to exactly those two. Kenji put it plainly — a fail would leave at least one of them evil, which is information, not camouflage. I agree with that read.

I also want to note something I haven't said yet, and I say it without accusation: rejecting this team would not remove Elena and Zara from the pool, and it would not put Lucia or Kenji on a mission instead of them. At five players, a revision swaps one name for another in a pair of two. The only thing a rejection buys is a reshuffle and one more round of the same argument, while costing us a proposal and sharpening the pattern I noted earlier — a table where the loudest objection can veto a leader's judgment with no evidence attached. If the pair is wrong, we will know it from the card, not from another speech.

So I am voting yes, and I will submit Success.

Elena, there is one thing still outstanding and it is the only reason I am speaking again. Arjun asked you a specific question — what in Zara's opening posture read as "steady," and would you give the same description to a player whose manner was warm but vague. Lucia has asked twice and has now built her entire case on the absence of an answer. That answer is genuinely useful to me and to Kenji, because if it turns out the word was a snap stylistic impression that applies to anyone, then the correct response is to discount it and move on; and if you saw something specific, then the whole table can use it going forward. Either answer ends this thread. Only silence keeps it alive, and at this point silence looks worse than either answer.

Elena, please answer that question directly — I yield the floor to you.

Arjun, you asked for the record, and you deserve a direct answer. “Steady” was not a claim that I had verified Zara’s loyalty or observed a mission-relevant action. It was a snap stylistic impression from her opening composure—calm and direct rather than performative. Would I use the same description for a player whose manner was warm but vague? Not exactly; warm-but-vague would read as affable but less defined. But I concede the word carried little evidentiary weight. That is why I did not treat it as proof, and why I have repeatedly said judge this team by the card. The table should discount “steady” going forward unless it is tied to specific behavior. I accept that correction. The team remains Elena and Zara because at five players any mission-one team is a pair, and the first real information is the pass or fail result. If it fails, the field narrows to us; if it passes, it is encouraging, not clearance. I am voting yes and will submit Success. Lucia’s objection has been heard, but my refusal to revise was not an attempt to dodge accountability—the vote and the mission card make both Zara and me directly accountable. I do not think continuing to litigate one adjective is useful now that I have answered it plainly.

Elena answered the question. That closes the only thread that was still open, and it closed in the way I hoped: she described "steady" as a snap stylistic impression, conceded it carried little evidentiary weight, and asked the table to discount it going forward unless tied to specific behavior. That is exactly the correction I was looking for, and I want to say plainly that Arjun's question has been answered and I am no longer treating the wording of the proposal as a live issue.

So the record stands where it should. On the evidence available to any of us — which is to say, no mission results and no private information about anyone — Elena and Zara is a legitimate team for mission one. At five players a two-person mission is the only possible size, and either outcome is informative: a pass confirms two specific people submitted Success, and a fail narrows the field immediately to those two. Kenji and Arjun have both said they would rather be on the team themselves but have no evidence-based reason to reject this pairing, and I agree with both of them. A revision here would mostly reshuffle one name for another and cost us a proposal and a round of the same argument.

Lucia, I want to be fair to you and also honest about where I land. Your challenge was legitimate procedure — a leader should be able to explain a choice, and a table should be able to ask. You did that, and you got an answer, and the answer was reasonable. You have also been clear that you will vote no on this pairing no matter how often it is resubmitted. That's your vote to cast and I won't pretend it is nothing; it does mean this team was approved with a dissent on record rather than by consensus. But it also means the dissent rests on a sentence the leader has now explained and retracted as evidence, and on a general suspicion of closed pairs that no result has yet supported. Refusing to revise on mission one, when any team is a pair and no evidence exists either way, is a defensible call, not a tell. I will not read it as one going forward.

I am voting yes on Elena and Zara and submitting Success. The team is Elena and Zara. Let the mission result speak, and let the next proposal be judged on what we actually learn rather than on how two people described an adjective. I'd rather we move forward now with a clear record than spend another proposal relitigating wording that has already been settled.

The discussion has run its course and the record is clear. Elena answered Arjun's question directly, conceded that "steady" was a snap impression rather than evidence, and asked the table to discount it going forward — that is exactly the kind of accountability Lucia said she was looking for. The substance of Lucia's objection has been addressed at every level: the team size is fixed at two for mission one at five players, both outcomes are informative, and neither Elena nor I has claimed special knowledge we don't have.

What remains is Lucia's pre-announced position that she will vote no on this pairing regardless of how many times it's resubmitted. That is her vote to cast, but it is worth naming what it represents: a decision made before the evidence she says she wants arrives. The mission card is the first real data point this table will get. Approving Elena and Zara gives us that data point immediately. Rejecting it costs a proposal and buys another round of the same argument with no new information.

Kenji, Arjun, and I have all said we have no evidence-based reason to reject this team, and Elena has answered every challenge put to her. I am voting yes on Elena and Zara. I'd ask the table to approve this team so we can get the mission result that everyone — including Lucia — has said they want to see. Let the card speak.

Elena confirms Elena, Zara. I am keeping Elena and Zara. The wording of “steady” has been addressed and discounted; the mission card is the first real evidence, so the table should judge this team by the result rather than another round of the same argument.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).
Kenji proposes Kenji, Arjun, Lucia. Mission 1 failed, so at least one of Elena and Zara is evil. This team excludes both and includes me, whose loyalty I know.

Kenji’s proposal is the right shape for mission two. Mission one failed with Elena and Zara, and I know what I submitted: Success. I cannot prove that to the table, but from my seat it means the fail card came from Zara. That is not comfortable to say about my mission-one partner, but the result is what it is. Zara spent much of the first discussion attacking Lucia for raising a legitimate process concern and demanding that we “let the card speak.” The card spoke: one fail. Since I submitted Success, the only consistent read available to me is that Zara is the source of that fail. I therefore support Kenji, Arjun, and Lucia. This team excludes both members of the failed mission-one team, so it does not ask the table to trust either of us. If it succeeds, that is useful; if it fails, the field narrows to the three people on it. I will vote yes. I would rather get a clean mission-two result than spend another proposal relitigating the first discussion. Zara can explain her own card if she wishes, but I am not going to pretend the failure did not happen or that my own submitted card was anything other than Success.

Elena says she submitted Success and immediately points at me. I'll be equally direct with the table: I submitted Success. If both of us are telling the truth, mission one would have passed. So one of us is lying, and neither claim carries more proof than the other — our mission cards are equally secret.

What strikes me is Elena's strategy. She supports a team that excludes both mission-one members, which means neither of us ever gets tested. If she genuinely believes I submitted the fail, the logical move is to put us on a mission together and let the table watch the result. Sidelining me while calling me guilty is conviction without trial.

Kenji, your proposed team is reasonable on its face, but it removes the two people who most need to prove themselves. Would you consider adding one of us, or do you believe excluding both suspects actually generates more information than testing them?

Zara, I am keeping Kenji, Arjun, and Lucia. At least one of you and Elena is evil, so excluding both gives this mission the best chance of success based on the result we have. Putting both of you together again would risk another failure without resolving which of you played the fail card. Putting one of you on the team could be considered later, but neither claim about the secret cards is independently verifiable. A success on this team would be encouraging, not proof that everyone on it is good.

Kenji, I support this team of you, Arjun, and myself, and I want to lay out why clearly.

Mission one failed with one fail card from a two-person team. That is the hardest fact on the table, and it tells us something concrete: at least one of Elena and Zara submitted Fail, which means at least one of them is lying right now, publicly, about having submitted Success. Both cannot be telling the truth. I won't pretend to know which claim is false — the cards are secret and neither claim is verifiable — but the contradiction itself is the most useful information we have gotten all game, and it makes one thing obvious: this mission should not include either of them.

Zara made an argument I want to address directly, because it sounds reasonable but isn't. She said that excluding both suspects means 'neither of us ever gets tested' and that putting the two of them on a mission together would let the table 'watch the result.' Think about what that actually buys us. If Elena and Zara go together and the mission fails, we learn nothing we don't already know — we already know at least one of them is evil. If it passes, Zara will claim exoneration, but two evil-aligned players can coordinate a pass just as easily as a fail when the game calls for it. A pass from that pair would be the weakest evidence in the game. Excluding both and running a clean team is strictly better: a success gives us a working baseline of three players we can build future teams around, and it isolates the fail card question to exactly the two people who were on mission one.

Elena's accusation of Zara and Zara's counter to Elena are both on the record. I'm not going to adjudicate between two secret-card claims, but I do note that Zara was the loudest voice demanding we 'let the card speak' in the first discussion — and when the card spoke, she immediately began arguing that the result shouldn't shape this team. That shift is worth something to me.

I'm voting yes on Kenji, Arjun, and Lucia. If this mission fails, the field narrows to three, and the two confirmed-linked suspects from mission one remain the priors.

Zara, you asked Kenji whether he'd consider adding one of you. He declined. My question to you is simpler: would you accept being excluded from this mission while still asserting you submitted Success on mission one — and if this team passes, will you drop the demand to be 'tested' and accept that the table is entitled to keep treating you as a suspect?

Lucia, you asked two questions and I'll answer both directly.

Yes, I accept being excluded if this table decides that's where the evidence points — but I want to name what's actually happening. Elena and I both publicly claimed Success on mission one. The math says one of us is lying. That is the only hard fact we have. But notice the asymmetry: Elena got to speak first, claimed Success, and immediately pointed at me. I was forced into the defensive position of responding to her accusation rather than the other way around. She chose the narrative; I inherited it.

What Elena did is strategically convenient for whoever actually submitted that fail card. If Elena is telling the truth, then yes, I'm the liar. But if Elena is the one who submitted Fail, then her accusation accomplishes exactly what an evil player would want: it puts suspicion on her partner while presenting herself as the honest one making a painful admission. Neither of us can prove our claim. The cards are secret. So Elena's confident accusation of me carries no more evidentiary weight than my claim of Success — it simply arrived first.

On your second question: if this team passes, I will not drop being a suspect. I am on mission one's failed team, and I will carry that suspicion until it's resolved. But I want to be clear that the same should apply symmetrically. Elena cannot present herself as having cooperated by throwing me under the bus and then be treated as cleared. If the table keeps both of us as suspects — which is fair — then this team correctly excludes us both. But nobody should treat Elena's accusation as established fact.

Kenji, your team of Kenji, Arjun, Lucia is reasonable given the constraint that at least one of Elena and Zara submitted Fail. If it passes, it tells us three people submitted Success. If it fails, it's genuinely surprising — all three should be good by current reasoning. Either result is useful. I'll vote on it honestly.

Zara yielded to me, so I'll take the floor and address the framing she just laid out, because it deserves a direct answer. Her argument is that Elena spoke first, claimed Success, and pointed at her, and that this sequencing means Elena 'chose the narrative' while Zara 'inherited it.' I want to push back on that carefully, because sequencing is not evidence, and I don't want this table adopting a rule that whoever accuses second is somehow more credible. The order of two unverifiable claims tells us nothing about which claim is false. What does tell us something is the substance around those claims. Zara spent the entire first discussion demanding that we 'let the card speak' — she said it multiple times, forcefully, and framed any hesitation as evasive. The card spoke. One fail. And the moment it did, Zara's position became that the result should not shape this team, that testing the mission-one pair would be meaningless, and that exclusion is 'conviction without trial.' That is a real shift in stated principle, and I noted it before and I note it again. At the same time, I want to be equally clear about the other side, because Zara is right about one thing: Elena's accusation of Zara is not proof either. Elena may have submitted Fail and is capitalizing on a convenient accusation. I cannot distinguish between two secret-card claims, and I won't pretend I can. The honest position is that both Elena and Zara are suspects, both should carry that suspicion symmetrically, and neither public claim of Success should be treated as clearance by anyone at this table. That is exactly why Kenji's team of Kenji, Arjun, and Lucia is the right construction. It excludes both suspects rather than gambling on either of their stories. If it passes, we gain a baseline of three players who submitted Success together, and the mission-one pair remains under suspicion — both of them, not one. If it fails, the field narrows to three and we've learned something painful but real. Either outcome moves us forward. Zara also conceded, to her credit, that she will not demand to be dropped from suspicion even if this team passes. I take that as stated in good faith, and I'll hold Elena to the identical standard: no accusation, no self-exoneration, no volunteer statement clears anyone. Only cards and results do. I'm voting yes on Kenji, Arjun, and Lucia, and I'd encourage the table to stop relitigating who spoke first and get the mission-two result we all need.

I support Kenji, Arjun, and Lucia. Mission 1 leaves at least one of Elena and Zara responsible for the fail; I know I submitted Success, so from my seat the fail came from Zara, but I agree with Lucia that neither of our public claims can be independently verified. That is exactly why the right move is to exclude both mission-one members and let a clean three-person team produce real evidence. If this team passes, it gives us a working baseline, though not absolute clearance for its members; if it fails, suspicion narrows to the three people on it. Zara’s argument that excluding both suspects is “conviction without trial” would keep the table relitigating the same failed pair instead of generating new information. I am not asking for a revision. I will vote yes on Kenji, Arjun, and Lucia.

I support Kenji, Arjun, and Lucia. The reasoning is straightforward: mission 1 failed, at least one of Elena and Zara is responsible, and this team excludes both of us while bringing in the three players with no mission-1 exposure. I have already said I accept being excluded while the table sorts out who submitted the fail card — I stand by that.

I want to address one thing briefly. Elena pointed at me; I pointed back. Neither claim can be verified, and I agree with Lucia that neither of us should be treated as cleared. 3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
